# Muni Sutta (Snp 1.12 (PTS Snp 35))
**ID:** Snp 1.12 (PTS Snp 35)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Muni Sutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp1.12
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Munisutta* ("The Sage", Snp 1.12) is the twelfth discourse of the Uragavagga in the *Suttanipāta* [SuttaCentral; Hazra 1994]. The poem describes the attributes of the ideal sage (*muni*), celebrating the solitary, wandering forest ascetic who finds peace and security far from domestic ties, overcomes spiritual obstacles, and has transcended speculative sophistry (*takka*) [SuttaCentral; Boucher 2008; Webster 2005]. Rhetorically, nine verses in the discourse conclude with the recurring refrain *taṃ vā pi dhīrā muniṃ vedayanti* ("him the wise declare to be a sage") [Katre 1931]. A well-known stanza contrasts the solitary forest mendicant with the householder using the simile of a wild goose or swan whose flight cannot be matched by a peacock [Lamotte 1988; Thich Thien Chau 1996]. The commentary (*Paramatthajotikā*) regards the sutta as an anthology of originally independent verses uttered by the Buddha on different occasions [Lamotte 1988].
Scholars generally identify the sutta with the *Munigāthā* mentioned in King Aśoka's Bhairat (Bhabru) edict among the texts recommended for reflection [SuttaCentral; Thomas 1933; Winternitz 1933; Wynne 2007]. Outside the Pali canon, Northern Buddhist literature such as the *Divyāvadāna* mentions the recitation of the *Munigāthā* alongside the *Śailagāthā* and the *Arthavargīya* [Hazra 1994], and the title is attested in Chinese transcriptions (*Mou-ni-chieh*) [Dhammapala et al. 1984]. In later Pali literature, the sutta is quoted in the *Milindapañha* (*Santhavapañha*, Mil 5.5.1, and *Vāyuṅgapañha*, Mil 7.4.4) [SuttaCentral]. Automatically detected text reuse in DharmaNexus confirms shared segments with the *Milindapañha* (Mil 5.5.1, §§1.1–1.4) and the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language alignments, DharmaNexus detects strong verse correspondences in the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu-avadāna* (highest plausibility score 85) as well as matches in the Tibetan *Udānavarga* and the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) [DharmaNexus; Nakamura 1980; Wynne 2007].
